title: Prometheus metrics in a Node service
bridge: A Prometheus counter is like a Redux counter that only goes up: you call inc() and never set it. Except: nobody reads it back in code. A scraper fetches the whole store every 30 seconds, and you ask for rates on the server, never for the raw value.
intro: The gateway counts every model call, the broker counts refused writes, and the nightly job writes delivery numbers. All of them speak Prometheus. This lesson adds a counter and a histogram to a Node service and exposes /metrics. It also explains when a job pushes instead of being scraped.

picture.caption: A service increments counters in memory; VMAgent scrapes /metrics on a timer and stores every series; Grafana asks the store for rates. A nightly job pushes with timestamps instead.

steps.text: costUsd.inc({ agent: "nova" }, 0.12) on every model answer
GET /metrics; the registry renders every series as text
writes the samples with the scrape time and the pod's labels
POST Prometheus text with millisecond timestamps for last night's and backfilled weeks

p: Open any /metrics endpoint and you see plain text: one line per series, a HELP and a TYPE comment above each metric. A series is a metric name plus a set of label values; the number after it is the current value. The gateway's two main series are below, in the shape G1-09 and G1-10 query.

Names end in _total for counters and carry the unit (usd, seconds, bytes). Labels split the number: agent, type. A label with thousands of values (a run id, a login) makes thousands of series, so labels stay few and never personal.
sections.because: We read the text format first because every tool in the chain speaks exactly this and nothing else. That means VMAgent, Grafana and the import endpoint.

code.text:
# HELP ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total Model spend in USD, from the gateway's usage accounting.
# TYPE ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total counter
ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total{agent="nova"} 184.2
ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total{agent="cifix"} 12.7
# HELP ai_agents_llm_tokens_total Tokens by type.
# TYPE ai_agents_llm_tokens_total counter
ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent="nova",type="input"} 4210033
ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent="nova",type="cache_read"} 31880120
ai_agents_llm_tokens_total{agent="nova",type="output"} 902114

notes.text: counter: only goes up. The store keeps every scraped value, so a rate over any window can be computed later.
One series: name plus labels. The value is the total since the process started, not since the last scrape.
The cache-read share in G1-09 is cache_read divided by input plus cache_read plus cache_write, from these series.

p: The Node library is @prometheus-io/client. It was published as prom-client until recently; npm now marks prom-client as replaced, so install the new name. You create a Registry and define a Counter with a name, a help text and label names. Then you call inc() with label values and an amount.

Define metrics once at module level and export them; the handler code only calls inc(). If the process restarts, counters start from zero again; that is fine, because the store computes rates across the reset.
sections.because: We count in the gateway because every model call passes through it. So the number is complete, whatever agent or laptop made the call.

notes.text: The README shows import * as client; use that form. Pin the exact version in package.json (0.16.1 today).
Our own registry instead of the global one, so tests can create a fresh one.
Default metrics are free and useful: memory growth and event-loop lag show a sick pod before users do.
Label names are fixed here; values come at inc() time. as const keeps the names typed.
inc(labels, amount). Amount defaults to 1; cost and tokens pass the real number.

p: A counter cannot tell you how long something took. A histogram counts observations into buckets: how many calls took under 1 s, under 5 s, under 30 s. From that the store estimates p50 or p95 with histogram_quantile. You choose the bucket edges to match what you care about.
On /metrics a histogram shows as several series: one _bucket per edge with an le label, plus _sum and _count. Grafana works on those.
sections.because: We use a histogram for model-call latency because the median hides a slow tail. The tail is where a stuck run shows first.

notes.text: No _total suffix: a histogram is not a counter. The unit (seconds) is in the name.
Edges in seconds, in increasing order. Pick edges where you would draw a line between fine and slow.
startTimer returns a function; calling it observes the time since start. observe(value) is the manual form.
Every observation adds 1 to _count, the value to _sum, and 1 to every bucket with le at or above it.

p: The library renders the registry as text; you serve it from your node:http server (p1-3) on a path the scraper knows. Keep it on a separate port from the API when you can, so the public route never exposes it. The content type matters: the scraper reads it to know the format.
sections.because: We expose /metrics on its own port because the gateway's API port is reachable by VMs, and metrics are for VMAgent only.

notes.text: 9464 is the port the OpenTelemetry Prometheus exporter uses by default; VMAgent's scrape config names it.
metrics() is async and renders every registered metric, defaults included, as the text you saw in the first section.
client.contentType is the Prometheus text content type with its version; the scraper parses by it.

sections.ifInstead: If instead you see an empty body with 200, no metric is registered on that registry. Check registers: [registry] on each metric, and check that you did not render the global registry by mistake.

sections.h: Pull or push: who starts the transfer
p: Prometheus is pull: the scraper visits each target on a timer. That fits long-running services, and VMAgent on inf already scrapes pods by annotation. A job that runs for two minutes at 02:20 is never up when the scraper comes, so it pushes instead.

G1-03's nightly job writes Prometheus text lines with a millisecond timestamp to VictoriaMetrics' import endpoint. It goes through the integration VMUser (a login for writing metrics), the way infrastructure's send-workflow-result.yml does. The timestamp is what puts a backfilled week on the right day instead of on the day the job ran.
sections.because: We push with explicit timestamps because the baseline is the 12 weeks before October. Those points must land on their own weeks.

code.file: ai-agents/metrics/src/vm.ts (sketch; the endpoint path is the one send-workflow-result.yml uses, check it there)

notes.text: The same Point tuple G1-07's weeklyPoints yields: name, labels, value, week timestamp.
Prometheus text with a trailing timestamp in milliseconds. Without it, the store would stamp the point with 'now'.
The import endpoint accepts this text. The real base URL and the VMUser token come from Secrets Manager via the OIDC role (p2-3).
A failed write must fail the job loudly; a silent gap in the baseline is worse than a red run.
One real line: team and quantile labels, a value in hours, a Monday 00:00 UTC timestamp.

callout.text: Pushed series are not counters. delivery_* values are already weekly numbers, so dashboards plot them as they are and never wrap them in rate().

sections.h: Naming and labels, the rules we keep
p: Prefix by owner: ai_agents_ for platform services, delivery_ for the nightly job, claude_code_ comes from the client. Unit in the name, _total on counters, snake_case always. Labels: agent, team, type, step, q, suite, version. Never login, email, run id or Jira key as a label on a scraped series; those belong in events.

Check the real names in vmui before writing a query. OTLP metrics arrive through the collector with Prometheus naming turned on, so what Claude Code calls claude_code.cost.usage becomes claude_code_cost_usage_USD_total.

callout.text: Why so strict about labels? Every distinct label combination is one series kept in memory and on disk. A login label on a per-call counter would make one series per person, per agent, per type. It would also make a dashboard that names people.

lab.title: A service with a counter and a histogram, scraped by curl

worked.do: mkdir metrics-lab && cd metrics-lab && npm init -y && npm pkg set type=module && npm install @prometheus-io/client@0.16.1 tsx@4.23.15

Write server.ts: a Registry with collectDefaultMetrics; a Counter lab_requests_total with labelNames ['agent']; a Histogram lab_request_seconds with buckets [0.01, 0.1, 1]; a node:http server on 9464 where GET /work?agent=<name> runs end = histogram.startTimer(), waits a random 0 to 200 ms, calls counter.inc({ agent }), end(), and answers 200 'ok'; GET /metrics answers registry.metrics() with client.contentType.

worked.see:
# HELP lab_requests_total ...
# TYPE lab_requests_total counter
# HELP lab_request_seconds ...
# TYPE lab_request_seconds histogram
(no samples yet: nothing was counted)

worked.do: for i in 1 2 3; do curl -s 'localhost:9464/work?agent=nova'; done; curl -s 'localhost:9464/work?agent=cifix'; echo

worked.see:
lab_requests_total{agent="nova"} 3
lab_requests_total{agent="cifix"} 1
lab_request_seconds_bucket{le="0.01"} 0
lab_request_seconds_bucket{le="0.1"} 2
lab_request_seconds_bucket{le="1"} 4
lab_request_seconds_bucket{le="+Inf"} 4
lab_request_seconds_sum 0.41
lab_request_seconds_count 4

lab.faded: Add a second counter lab_errors_total{agent} and make GET /work?agent=<name>&fail=1 increment it and answer 500. Call it twice and scrape. The curl line that proves both counters moved is yours to write.
lab.alone: Write push.ts with the writePoints function from the lesson and point it at http://localhost:8428 (nothing is listening yet). Run it, read the error it throws, then start VictoriaMetrics with docker run --rm -p 8428:8428 victoriametrics/victoria-metrics:latest and run push.ts again. Open http://localhost:8428/vmui and query delivery_review_wait_hours; the point should sit on the timestamp you sent, not on now.
lab.done: curl shows lab_requests_total per agent and the histogram's buckets, sum and count. A pushed point appears in vmui at its own timestamp.

quiz.q: The gateway pod restarts and ai_agents_llm_cost_usd_total drops from 184 to 0. Is the day's spend lost?

options.text: Yes; you must persist counters to disk.
options.why: Counters live in memory by design; the store already holds every scraped value.

options.text: No; the store saw every value and increase() handles the reset.
options.why: Prometheus-style stores treat a drop as a reset and add the pieces when computing rate or increase.

options.text: Only if VMAgent scraped in the last 30 seconds.
options.why: You lose at most the un-scraped tail of one interval, not the day.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good label for a scraped counter in the gateway?

options.why: One series per ticket, forever; the run token carries the ticket, and events hold that detail.
A handful of values, meaningful to split by, and never a person.
Personal and high-cardinality; no dashboard has a person dimension.

quiz.q: Why does the nightly job push with millisecond timestamps instead of serving /metrics?

options.text: Because pushing is faster than scraping.
options.why: Speed is not the point; the job is not running when a scraper would visit.

options.text: Because it runs for minutes at 02:20 and backfills 12 weeks, so each point must land on its own week.
options.why: A scrape would stamp everything with the scrape time; explicit timestamps put the baseline where it belongs.
VMAgent scrapes every pod on inf; the job is the exception, not the store.

words.plain: One metric name with one set of label values; each distinct combination is its own line on /metrics.
A metric that only goes up; you call inc() and let the store compute rates.
Counts observations into buckets (le edges) plus _sum and _count, so the store can estimate p50 or p95.
The in-memory set of metrics that metrics() renders as text.
A timed GET of /metrics by VMAgent; pull, not push.
VictoriaMetrics' write path for Prometheus text with timestamps, used by jobs that are not up to be scraped.
How many distinct label combinations a metric has; keep it small, never a person.

tickets.why: The nightly job writes Prometheus text with millisecond timestamps to VictoriaMetrics: the push half of this lesson.
weeklyPoints yields the Point tuples that writePoints turns into lines.
The spend view and the burn-rate alert read the gateway's counters by agent and the job's ai_spend_* series.
The gateway's token and cost series must carry the step label set by the harness.

remember: Counters go up, histograms bucket, and /metrics is scraped on a timer. A job that is not alive at scrape time pushes text with its own timestamps.
